abstract: Dr. Jon Calvert discusses the evaluation and management of adnexal masses, emphasizing the importance of classifying masses as neoplastic or nonneoplastic. Nonneoplastic masses include functional cysts (follicular and corpus luteum) and organic pathologies (endometrioma, tubo-ovarian abscess). He reviews bimanual examination technique, noting that uterine position affects palpation, and that the ovary is roughly the size of the distal thumb phalanx. Ultrasound findings of simple versus complex cysts guide management, with simple cysts having a 90% chance of benignity and often resolving spontaneously. Key clinical pearls include the need for endometrial monitoring in PCOS, observation of hemorrhagic cysts, and prompt antibiotic therapy for tubo-ovarian abscess.
key_points: Adnexal masses are divided into neoplastic (benign or malignant) and nonneoplastic; common nonneoplastic masses include follicular cysts, corpus luteum cysts, endometriomas, and tubo-ovarian abscesses.
Bimanual exam technique: place fingers in the posterior fornix and lift; if the uterus is retroverted, the fundus may not be felt because the cervix is pushed forward instead.
Ovary size equals the distal phalanx of the thumb; in obese women, ovaries are often not palpable, and in postmenopausal women they become even smaller.
On ultrasound, a simple cyst (anechoic, thin-walled) has a 90% chance of being benign; complex cysts (loculated or with solid excrescences) require further workup.

PCOS diagnosis requires irregular menses, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound; management includes ensuring endometrial shedding at least once a year to prevent hyperplasia and screening for diabetes.
Functional cysts (follicular, corpus luteum) are common and often resolve spontaneously; simple cysts less than 10 cm can be followed with repeat ultrasound in 3 months.
Hemorrhagic ovarian cyst presents with acute pain near ovulation and shows internal echoes/clot on ultrasound; management is observation, not surgery.
Tubo-ovarian abscess from PID requires IV antibiotics; fertility prognosis is guarded due to tubal damage.
In postmenopausal women, any palpable ovary should be evaluated with ultrasound, as it may indicate malignancy.
Timing of pelvic pain in relation to menstrual cycle is critical: mid-cycle pain (Mittelschmerz) is benign and self-limited.
